title: How Plaid Survived on K Before Becoming Fintech Infrastructure | Zach Perret
question: In software platform startups, what actually happens to day-to-day business performance during a long pending acquisition review?
guest: As with all startups, especially platform businesses, you do a bunch of work, and then at some point in the future the work pays off. That point could be six months, two years, or three years, depending on the things you built. Clearly we'd built a set of good products, and then market demand really increased for those products, so we were growing really fast during that period. I think the restrictions on the business during that period were largely around hiring. We did hire a lot of people, but it's hard to express to super entrepreneurial people the upside potential of a business if it clearly has a transaction hanging over it. So I would say we were a little restricted in who we could hire. We were a little restricted on the press that we could do. But I would say we were maybe not firing at a hundred percent, probably firing at ninety-five percent, and the underlying numbers of the business were just up and to the right, so we felt pretty good about it.

points.note: Accept: difficulty pitching standalone equity upside or attracting high-agency builders while a buyout is pending. Do not credit: vague mentions of general employee distraction or cultural clash.

points.core: Pending deal scrutiny restricts the external press a startup can publicly generate.

models.answer:
There is no single outcome, but the usual pattern is a slow drag rather than a collapse. This rests on well-known cases and general M&A knowledge; my one search turned up no systematic study of this specific question.

During a long review the startup must keep operating independently, because antitrust "gun-jumping" rules bar integration with the buyer. Meanwhile, the merger agreement's interim covenants typically restrict it from raising capital, making big hires, changing pricing or doing its own deals without buyer consent.

The result is that routine metrics often hold up while strategic momentum stalls. Customers hesitate over long-term contracts because the roadmap is uncertain, and competitors exploit that in sales pitches. Key employees get distracted or leave as their retention payouts sit in limbo. Management attention shifts to regulators' document requests.

How much damage this does depends on underlying strength. Figma kept growing strongly through Adobe's roughly 15-month review and came out healthy with a $1 billion breakup fee. iRobot, already weakening and reliant on Amazon's deal closing, deteriorated badly and cut staff heavily when it collapsed. Sticky, fast-growing platforms tend to coast, while fragile ones erode.

noweb.answer:
Performance usually degrades, often quietly at first. The startup must keep operating as an independent competitor, but the deal's interim covenants restrict major moves such as large hires, pricing changes, new financing, big contracts and pivots without the buyer's consent, and antitrust "gun-jumping" rules prevent the two companies from coordinating. So the company is stuck executing a standalone plan that nobody fully believes in anymore.

The practical effects compound over time. Enterprise customers delay renewals and new purchases because they are unsure about the roadmap, and competitors exploit that uncertainty in sales cycles. Partners and integrators hedge. Employees get distracted, recruiting gets harder, and attrition rises among key engineers and salespeople, especially if retention packages only pay out at closing. Leadership attention goes to regulators, document requests and integration planning rather than product. Roadmap decisions get deferred, so product velocity slows.

Meanwhile, cash burn continues, and fundraising is typically off the table. If the deal ultimately collapses, as with Figma and Adobe, the company can recover, but it often emerges with lost momentum and a need to reset, sometimes cushioned by a breakup fee.

During a prolonged acquisition review, a software platform startup operates in strategic limbo: recurring revenue often holds up in the near term, but growth velocity and agility degrade. Antitrust gun-jumping rules force the company to operate independently, while merger covenants restrict it to ordinary-course operations, effectively freezing bold pivots, pricing overhauls, fundraising, and hiring surges without buyer consent.

Day to day, regulatory discovery and integration planning consume heavy executive bandwidth. Externally, enterprise customers and third-party developers often hesitate to sign multi-year contracts or build deep integrations, fearing post-close price hikes, API deprecation, or competitive conflicts with the acquirer, creating uncertainty that rivals actively exploit. Internally, recruiting slows because equity upside is capped, while existing employees often split between attrition and coasting while awaiting a payout.

Performance ultimately diverges by business model. Platforms with entrenched product-led adoption and high switching costs, like Figma or Plaid, can keep shipping incremental features and compounding usage, whereas sales-led or cash-burning startups frequently see pipelines, partner ecosystems, and product execution stall.

noweb.answer:
During a prolonged acquisition review, a software platform startup typically enters an operational limbo where growth decelerates and execution shifts from offense to preservation. Merger agreements impose strict interim operating covenants that restrict major spending, pricing changes, senior hiring, and strategic pivots without the buyer’s consent, while leadership’s attention is diverted toward regulatory requests and integration planning.

On the commercial front, enterprise sales cycles lengthen as prospective customers and third-party ecosystem partners hesitate, fearing roadmap changes, broken integrations, or ownership by a competitor. High switching costs usually keep existing renewals steady, temporarily masking a weaker new-business pipeline and slower ecosystem expansion. Internally, productivity and morale dip as employees wait in financial uncertainty; rival recruiters target key engineers and salespeople, while hiring strong replacements becomes difficult once equity upside is capped at the deal price. Consequently, product velocity often narrows to safe, incremental updates rather than bold platform bets. The business rarely collapses outright, but compounding friction erodes momentum, leaving the startup with lost market ground to rebuild if the deal ultimately falls through.

Usually the business slows down, though it rarely collapses. The merger agreement includes interim operating covenants that require the target to run "in the ordinary course." In practice it often needs the buyer's consent for big hires, pricing changes, new financing, major partnerships or large contracts. So strategic moves tend to pause even while normal operations continue.

Customers and partners hesitate. Enterprise buyers may delay multi-year commitments until they know who will own the product, and competitors use that uncertainty in their sales pitches. Employees are the biggest risk. Recruiting gets harder, and key engineers often leave if equity payouts look uncertain or the deal drags on, so firms commonly add retention bonuses.

Results vary. Figma kept growing strongly during Adobe's roughly 15-month review, and when regulators killed the deal in 2023 it collected a $1 billion breakup fee. Smaller targets with less cash, like iRobot after Amazon dropped its bid, can come out much weaker.

Overall, revenue tends to hold steady while hiring, product ambition and morale decline. The longer the review lasts, the larger the cost if the deal falls through.

noweb.answer:
During a long acquisition review, the startup usually keeps operating independently. Customers still pay their subscriptions, support tickets get answered, and engineering keeps shipping. That recurring revenue can make the business look steady even as growth starts to slow.

Uncertainty tends to show up first in decisions people can postpone. Prospects delay signing while they wait to see what happens to pricing, the product roadmap, or support. Partners hold off on integrations, candidates hesitate to join, and employees may leave. Executives spend time on the review, and some hiring or investment decisions take longer. Those effects often show up in new bookings, expansion revenue, and hiring before they show up in total revenue.

A startup with loyal customers, enough cash, and a team that can keep making decisions may sustain its pace. One that depends on a few large deals, key hires, or fresh funding can lose months of momentum while the review is still pending.

points.why: The response attributes steady revenue to existing subscriptions without linking growth during the review to the delayed payoff of earlier platform investments.
The response mentions candidate hesitation without explaining how the pending acquisition makes standalone equity upside harder to pitch to entrepreneurial hires.
The response does not identify any limits on press coverage, public announcements, or other external communications during the review.

During a long acquisition review, the startup still runs independently. Customers keep using the platform, subscriptions renew, and engineers keep shipping. The uncertainty tends to matter most when someone has to make a new commitment. A customer may renew existing seats but delay a company-wide rollout until pricing and product plans are clearer. A job candidate may hesitate to join, and executives handling the review have less time for customers and staff. Revenue can therefore keep growing even as some decisions take longer.

Figma illustrates how much can continue. During the 15-month review of Adobe’s proposed acquisition, Figma released new FigJam features and continued to grow. How much faster or slower it would have grown without the review is unknown. noweb.answer:
During a long acquisition review, the startup usually keeps operating independently. Customers still use the platform, subscriptions renew, and revenue may keep growing. The slowdown often shows up first in decisions about the future. A customer may postpone a rollout until it knows whether the buyer will support the product. A developer may hold off on building an integration, or an engineer may leave because their role after the deal is unclear. Managers also spend time answering review requests, and the deal agreement may require the buyer’s consent for unusually large commitments.

These effects can take months to reach reported revenue. Sales cycles, new integrations, hiring, and product releases can show strain earlier. There’s no universal decline, though. A startup can keep growing throughout the review, and slower growth alone doesn’t establish how much the review caused.

The response mentions hiring strain and uncertainty about roles but never explains how a pending buyout makes it harder to attract entrepreneurial talent by limiting perceived equity upside.
